routes.description: Establish historical reliability through a cumulative standard that permits ordinary reporting variation while requiring substantial accuracy across the Gospels' claims.
routes.successCriteria: Show that verified or conceded claims at several levels outweigh alleged errors and that prominent discrepancies can arise from historically permissible conventions or reconcilable sequences.

motionBridge.description: The Gospels remain historically reliable if their supported historical content is not counterbalanced by established errors.

centralBridges.description: Identify substantial accurate content among major, intermediate, and lesser Gospel claims.
Show that the principal birth and resurrection differences do not negate the shared central claims or require incompatible histories.
Establish a historically supportable continuity between Synoptic material and claims about Jesus' elevated or divine identity.
Provide a plausible account of how traditions and sources preserved the essential events and teachings reported by the evangelists.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish selection, paraphrase, topical ordering, and approximation from factual contradiction.
Connect disputed material to eyewitnesses, remembered traditions, or sources close to eyewitness testimony.

routes.description: Establish historical unreliability in important respects by locating conflicts or inventions in major narratives and sayings rather than merely peripheral details.
routes.successCriteria: Show that major birth, resurrection, and self-presentation material cannot all be historically accurate and that authorial reshaping or unstable transmission explains the divergences.

motionBridge.description: The Gospels are historically unreliable in important respects if major reported events or sayings contain unresolved conflicts or nonhistorical material.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate materially incompatible historical sequences within the canonical birth narratives.
Demonstrate materially incompatible locations, instructions, or actions within the resurrection narratives.
Show that John's divine self-presentation lacks adequate continuity with earlier Synoptic portrayals of Jesus.
Connect Gospel divergences to evangelists altering inherited material for distinct theological messages and audiences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Assess whether narrow or nonindependent attestation weakens disputed claims.
Account for how decades of oral transmission and later composition could change reported events or sayings.

sections.title: Standard and cumulative case for reliability
sections.rationale: The governing definition of historical reliability determines whether conceded accuracy across much of Jesus' life can be outweighed by conflicts involving several major narratives or sayings.

sections.title: Historical compatibility of the birth narratives
sections.rationale: Matthew and Luke are the canonical sources that narrate Jesus' birth, so the compatibility and provenance of their family movements bear directly on a principal alleged instance of unreliability.

sections.title: Compatibility of the resurrection accounts
sections.rationale: The resurrection is a central Gospel claim, making the chronology and locations of the women's report, appearances, and disciples' movements material to the reliability question.

sections.title: Jesus' self-presentation and divine identity
sections.rationale: Whether John's divine self-identifications preserve Jesus' historical teaching depends partly on whether earlier Synoptic traditions contain comparable claims, directly or indirectly.

sections.title: Ancient composition and transmission
sections.rationale: The reliability inference depends on whether variation reflects permissible ancient reporting and stable preservation or instead historical invention, changing oral tradition, and message-driven alteration.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Although the Gospels preserve a reliable basic outline of Jesus' life, numerous inconsistencies and nonhistorical accounts make them historically unreliable in important respects.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Bart Ehrman's opening statement, and this passage continues uninterrupted within that announced turn.

response.rationale: This constructive states the governing concession and contrary thesis: broad outline reliability can coexist with important historical unreliability where major conflicts or nonhistorical accounts remain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: As a constructive thesis, it clearly frames the controlling standard and the principal categories of support to follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition and concession are explicit, though “large numbers” and “unreliable” remain somewhat broad until illustrated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The express concession about the basic outline appropriately limits the force of the broader unreliability claim.

charity.alternative: Substantial agreement on the basic outline may justify calling the Gospels historically reliable overall.
charity.decisiveQualification: The thesis limits its challenge to important respects grounded in alleged major conflicts and nonhistorical material.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between a reliable outline and unreliability in important respects is coherent and avoids an all-or-nothing inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The opening thesis previews concrete categories but does not itself establish their number, importance, or historical status.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly articulates the con motion bridge and the condition under which important unreliability follows.

representationalCharity.rationale: It expressly grants the strongest favorable point while explaining why that concession does not settle important disputed content.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes the basic Gospel story while alleging numerous inconsistencies, contradictions, and nonhistorical accounts.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives give incompatible accounts of the family's original home, travel, census, flight to Egypt, and eventual settlement in Nazareth.
moves.attributionBasis: This extended comparison occurs continuously during Bart Ehrman's moderator-announced opening statement and follows his own transition to the birth narratives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a concrete, temporally framed example central to the birth-narrative route rather than merely asserting divergence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenged sequence is recoverable and specific, although the inference assumes each author presents a sufficiently exhaustive itinerary.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The textual juxtaposition is strong, but incompatibility requires defending the assumption that omitted intervals or residences are excluded.

charity.alternative: The accounts may select different episodes and permit an unmentioned Egypt interval or more than one residence.
charity.decisiveQualification: A reconciliation must still explain Luke’s apparently direct return and Matthew’s distinct home-and-settlement framing without merely adding possibilities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The chronological comparison supports tension, with one bounded bridge needed from narrative sequence and omission to strict incompatibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites concrete events and timing, but representative textual details supporting every asserted conflict are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable conflict required by the con birth bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument fairly identifies the harmonizing burden, though it does not fully examine selection or dual-residence alternatives.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The resurrection narratives cannot all be reconciled regarding whether the women reported the empty tomb and whether the disciples remained in Jerusalem or traveled to Galilee.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Bart Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement and is clearly introduced by his transition from the birth accounts to resurrection accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It presents concrete narrative actions and locations that directly instantiate the claimed resurrection incompatibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The accounts create substantial prima facie tension, while categorical impossibility requires excluding sequential appearances and selective narration.

charity.alternative: Appearances could occur first in Jerusalem and later in Galilee, with each Gospel selecting different episodes.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reconciliation must accommodate Luke’s stay-in-Jerusalem instruction and the apparent narrative timing, not merely combine all reported events.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central con resurrection bridge with disputed locations, instructions, and actions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move exposes the strongest textual pressure on harmonization but states impossibility before fully excluding a multi-stage sequence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts reporting by the women and the Galilee expectation in Mark and Matthew with the differing Lukan trajectory.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: John's extensive divine self-identification by Jesus is historically doubtful because multiple earlier Synoptic sources do not portray him making comparable claims.
moves.attributionBasis: This is the concluding argument of Bart Ehrman's explicitly announced opening statement, ending immediately before applause and the moderator's speaker change.

response.rationale: This constructive argues from the absence of comparable explicit divine self-identification across several earlier Synoptic source strata to doubt about John’s historical presentation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a clear comparative-attestation argument directed to the central self-presentation issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source comparison is recoverable, although “calling himself God” may exclude indirect or differently expressed elevated claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the silence odd is appropriately probabilistic, but the argument compresses dependence among sources and genre or thematic selection.

charity.alternative: The Synoptics may express Jesus’ divine status indirectly rather than through John’s explicit first-person formulations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indirect elevated claims would weaken a simple silence argument but would not automatically authenticate John’s extensive distinctive speeches.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidential-silence inference is coherent but needs fuller treatment of source independence, expected mention, and indirect equivalents.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple earlier strata are named, but their independence and the absence of comparable material are asserted more than demonstrated here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con bridge requiring inadequate continuity between John and earlier Synoptic portrayals.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument fairly focuses on comparable self-identification, though its formulation underplays the strongest indirect-continuity case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names Mark, Q, M, and L as earlier sources and argues their failure to report comparable divine self-speech is historically significant.

moves.speaker: Jimmy Akin
moves.proposition: Historical reliability is distinct from inerrancy and may be established through many verified major, intermediate, and lesser claims unless contrary errors outweigh them.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues within Jimmy Akin's moderator-announced opening statement, with consistent first-person framing and no indication of a speaker change.

components.text: Whether important alleged errors outweigh the conceded accurate outline and other verifiable claims.

moves.proposition: Agreement on many general facts does not establish Gospel reliability because conflicts concerning the virgin birth, resurrection, and Jesus' self-presentation concern major claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The answer reaches the decisive weighting premise and names the specific disputed subjects claimed to be major.

components.text: Whether narrative differences negate the shared major claim that Jesus was resurrected.
Whether resurrection disagreements concern the major claim itself or surrounding matters.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the consequence and classification arguments but does not resolve the specific Jerusalem-Galilee or women-reporting conflicts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited proposition is clear: shared affirmation survives differences, without claiming that every surrounding report is accurate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Shared affirmation does preserve one claim, but saying differences therefore must be lesser assumes a debatable hierarchy of historical importance.

charity.alternative: Conflicting locations and instructions may be major historical defects even if every Gospel affirms resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Agreement on resurrection establishes convergence only on the top-line claim, not accuracy of each narrative account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The shared-core inference is valid within its scope, but the move does not justify the further claim that all disagreements are minor.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Unanimous Gospel affirmation is specifically stated, while the historical independence and evidential value of that agreement remain unaddressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro discrepancy bridge by preserving the shared resurrection claim despite narrative variation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response acknowledges differences but materially compresses the strongest objection by treating all surrounding matters as necessarily lesser.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that all four Gospels affirm resurrection and classifies their differences as below the top-line major claim.

moves.speaker: Jimmy Akin
moves.proposition: Ancient Gospel accounts ordinarily convey an accurate gist with approximate details, so evaluating them as if they promised modern precision can generate false contradictions.
moves.attributionBasis: Jimmy Akin continues his rebuttal with an extended approximation analogy and explicitly applies the resulting gist principle to the evangelists.

components.text: Whether the specific alleged inconsistencies and nonhistorical accounts are substantial enough to establish unreliability.

response.rationale: The move offers relevant contrary material about ancient precision and gist, but it does not apply that convention to a particular alleged conflict or show that the challenged birth, resurrection, or self-presentation differences are approximations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong relevant nonanswer because it supplies a potentially important convention without contacting the thesis’s decisive examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The gist principle is clear, but “accurate gist” and the range of details legitimately treated as approximate are left broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ancient approximation is plausible, but the move generalizes from cultural expectations without establishing its application to the disputed passages.

charity.alternative: Some Gospel differences concern incompatible events or instructions, not merely numerical or verbal precision.
charity.decisiveQualification: A convention defense must identify what each evangelist intended to approximate and why the shared gist remains accurate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The principle coherently distinguishes approximation from error, while its relevance to the selected disputes requires an unstated application bridge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary conventions tier, it strongly advances the distinction between approximate reporting and factual contradiction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The warning against modern precision is fair, but the strongest conflict argument is weakened by grouping unlike discrepancies under approximation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts modern transcript-level expectations with evangelists’ intended gist accounts and different levels of approximation.

moves.speaker: Jimmy Akin
moves.proposition: The birth accounts can be reconciled if Joseph had connections or property in Bethlehem while living and working in Nazareth before the family's later return there.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Akin's direct answer during Ehrman's cross-examination, with the alternating questions and responses clearly identifying the speaker.

components.text: Whether Matthew and Luke require incompatible original homes and movements for Joseph’s family.

response.rationale: The proposed Bethlehem family property and Nazareth work residence directly contacts the home-and-movement component by supplying a scenario under which both narrative framings could be true.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive component and establishes logical compatibility, but does not answer the census, Egypt, forty-day return, or settlement-sequence demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reconciliation is specific and repeatedly framed as Akin’s historical proposal rather than a fact established by the texts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speculative dual-residence hypothesis is presented cautiously enough for its limited compatibility purpose.

charity.alternative: Joseph’s economic status and the narrative framing make ownership or maintenance of two residences historically unlikely.
charity.decisiveQualification: Logical possibility does not establish historical probability without textual or socioeconomic support for the second residence.

moves.proposition: A lower-class manual laborer in first-century Palestine would be unlikely to maintain residences in both Bethlehem and Nazareth, making that reconciliation historically implausible.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage follows Akin's answer and uses first-person evaluation and a new question in Ehrman's established cross-examination turn.

components.text: Whether a low-income manual laborer plausibly maintained property or residences in both Bethlehem and Nazareth.
